INTERVIEW WITH RUSSELL "BIG CHIEF" MOORE
THE INSTITUTE OF JAZZ STUDIES
RUTGERS UNIVERSITY, NEWARK, NEW JERSEY
RON WELBURN, INTERVIEWER
Cassette One

For the record, this is the interview with Russell Moore, Russell "Big Chief" Moore, for the Jazz Oral History Project at The Institute of Jazz Studies at Rutgers University in Newark, New Jersey. My name's Ron Welburn, and I'm coordinating the project, and I'm a guest in the home of Russell Moore and his family.
Russell, good morning.
Good morning, Ron.
We're pleased to have you as a part of the oral history project.
I think that's wonderful.
Ok. Russell, could you tell us -- start by telling us something of your early life? You were born on the Pima Reservation at Komatkee, Gill Crossing.
Right.
Could you tell us something of your early life and childhood there, your earliest involvement -- leading to your earliest involvement in music.

Yes. The best of my recollection, I've always been musical ever since first awakenings about when I was about six years old when I used to go to an old man by the name of Skomuck on the reservation. He was in his ninties,

and a bunch of us kids would bring different gifts like maybe a sack of beans, corn, tobacco, and we'd go over and listen to him sing the chants of the Pimas. And we would listen to the stories of the early days of Pima land in early years when they used to -- the tribe used to fight with the Apaches, and the Pimas would fight with the Apaches and the constant turmoil there in the old days. And where the music part comes in is they have -- the Indians have songs that were depicted through battle songs, and I think everybody -- everyone in the early years is always -- have some conection with rhythm, melody. And even the -- go back to the Black tribes of -- African tribes, they have beautiful rhythm and song. And I can vouch for my tribe. We had rhythm and song too. And when we visited old Skomuck, we would just, out of respect for an old man who, who still followed the tribal chants and things like we, we would sit around close to him, and he would sing to us. That's the first time when I was six years old that I heard the chants of the Pima. And to this day, in all these years, I can still hear old Skomuck laying in his house on a blanket and treating us to his chants and his stories of Indian folklore. And that was my first awakening of music in my soul 'cause, as I said, to this day I can still sing the chants that old Skomuck used to sing to us kids. And one time we were at Skomuck listening to his singing and his chanting, and he kept us so long that we were -- we wouldn't tell him to stop, we're going home. We just
silently stole out of his adobe house, and we could still hear him although we were far away out to in our home. And we had quite a, quite a lot of experience with old Skomuck.

So, you learned your tribal songs and a -- and even the dances first. And that carried you a -- into when you started school you were able to play musical and various instruments, any pipes, or did you have an early beginning of an education in music at that time?
A--, yes. Would you like a sample of what the songs that Skomuck taught me in my early years?
Can you sing them?
Oh, of course I can.
Sure, go ahead.
Would you like a little taste of the Pima?
Yea! That would be very good!

Oh, thank you. The title of this song is "Schulduck Mahmu " -- translated in English it's "Water Babies", and it describes how the little birds along the Gila River when they used to have water. Of course it's a wash now. They'd -- they'd be flying low over the water, drinking it or bathing in it -- the little birds -- and that's the song about the birds. And this is the way it goes.
SINGS

Very beautiful. That's -- I'm sure that a song like that and a -- and a kind of a melody and the flavor that that melody has has appeared in some of your work as you became a professional musician. Would you feel -- do you feel that some of that a, that feeling and that melody has come up in things that you've played over the years in various orchestras when you've been playing with people like Buster Bailey and Henry "Red" Allen?

Oh yes, yes, yes, yes. I learned the art of projection -- to project to the listeners in the audience by watching the great musicians that I have worked with. As you say Buster Bailey and "Red" Allen and Louis Armstrong and many, many greats that I can't a -- I could mention, I mean in the short space of time like we -- like here. I have worked with many. I've learned how to, how to get that rhythm and also the blues and sing things like "Basin Street", "Saint James Infirmary". And some on my albums are -- are on the albums when I made them. And a -- I had quite a lot of fun doing a, doing -- learning the process of how to project and listen to other people sing -- that's the way I learned. I think everybody learns by listening to other people. I always loved to hear either Jack Teagarden or a, or a -- any of the big bands or big name musicians that a -- and there are some musicians that are lesser known, that are not -- haven't been found yet that you can -- sometimes you go into clubs and listen to. And

you learn a few things from somebody that is unknown. You'd be surprised how many I've listened to that I have never heard name mentioned before, and you know who they are. I go to a club; I listen, and I get things like that.

I see. When you were a boy living in Arizona, did very many people have in your reservation or in your community or places near where you went to school have victrolas, the record players, and did they have records of, say, some of the things that a -- maybe rag time music or cake walk music?

Yes. First of all, on my, on my reservation there's a school there by the name of St. John's Mission. And during the late '20s, they had a band there -- a military band. They used to march. And I always went over on the days that they had band concerts and a -- or the parades, and I would go home and imitate the St. John's Mission band. There weren't too many records that the Indians had in them years. And a radio wasn't quite a -- see we didn't have electricity when a -- oh during those early years -- that the time I was six and seven and that in a way I have learned just by my own, my own awareness to music and listening to that school band at St. John's Mission. And that's how I learned a lot of my music.
Those instruments you used to imitate this music that you heard the military band, they were home-made instruments?

Anything I would pick up that had a hole through it -- like a pipe or a -- or have a -- improvise a mouth piece of some kind and a, just make any kind of, kind of noise that would make some kind of melody and a -- I used to have a habit. When I walk I would sing. And when I sing I would keep time to the steps of my feet while I, while I was stepping a, a -- you know . . .
You sang tribal songs or other songs, popular songs?
Any song that came by a -- either popular songs or the band music from St. John's Mission or the tribal -- the one that I just sang a while back.
What were -- you remember any of your favorite songs at that time?

My favorite songs were anything that would pertain a melody. During them years, I cannot recall just what , what the melodies were, but , my memory -- not so, not so keen about the titles of the songs, but whatever heard -- whenever heard, I, I have, I remember the melody but I couldn't tell you at this time , just the titles of the songs that I heard there.

Before you left Arizona, did -- do you remember any of the famous a -- say military or marching bands that came through? I don't know whether the Sousa band or whether the Arthur Prior orchestra ever came through there, but were
there other, I'm sure, military orchestras? Were they big favorites on the reservation?

Well, during those early years, I wasn't exposed to any big name like John Philip Sousa or Prior or any of the military. You see I was, I was pretty well on the reservation, and you don't get out to hear -- listen to any, any of that, but whatever is exposed to us -- just, just that -- St. John's Mission Band and a once in a while you hear somebody have a record of something -- of one of the tunes or whatever orchestras or bands there were. I can't remember to this time. But most of it was the military band at St. John's where I learned how to -- how to sing and walk a -- the singing.
Did you start studying any of the instruments like the trumpet or the cornet or French horn before you left Arizona?

Yes, when I went to the Phoenix Indian School in 1923. That's where I first picked up the trumpet. And, incidentally, when I picked up the trumpet, it always slipped to one side of my embouchure. And that's how I happen to this day play on the side of my mouth.
That's the right side, huh?

Yea! And when, when now -- I've gone to teachers that have -- different musicians have told me and said why don't you go to a teacher and correct that up there. So I go to the teacher, and the teacher looks at me, and he asks

me to play something. So the teacher's found -- a few of the teachers when I went to take lessons to correct that -- put it in the center of my mouth -- blow in the center of my mouth. They would tell me stay there; it sounds better on that side. So I never got to changing my embouchure.
I see. Ok. What, what led up to, what brought about your leaving Arizona? Your father passed at that time; wasn't it?

Yes. In 1924 I was twelve-years-old, and my father passed away. And it was a sad ocassion, of course, to have, to have a funeral at the church where all the activities are. This happened on Fourth of July. You see in those years, there was no embalmers around, and when, when a, a body -- when somebody dies, you'll have to bury him in the, in the -- right away. So, in that way, when my father died, that's when I left Chicago --I, I don't mean Chicago. I left to go to Chicago when my uncle in Chicago said bring the two younquest boys up here and we'll send them to school. That's how I got to Chicago.
That was you, and who was the other brother?
Ah, my brother Everett who was younger than me, about six years younger. We were, we were the ones that were sent to Chicago.
Where actually was that it was -- that you were living?
Just precisely where did -- it was a little suburb, wasn't it?

Yes, it was. In South Chicago had a little town called Blue Island, and that's where we were raised there in a, right in a, right in Blue Island by the Rock Island Line right from LaSalle Street Station.
What kind of community was that? Who lived there? You know, was it a black community, white community, a mixed community, or, or what?

It was all mixed. I'll never understand how I just left the reservation and I'm not exposed to any of these scenes that I saw when I first went to school. To see a black student and a white student and a Latin student here, and we're not -- I wasn't aware of It was strange to me to, to see that. It was quite a while, a month or two, when I got used to everything there and made friends and made non-friends also too. You make friends and that other type of friends too.
Ok, your uncle's name was William T. Moore. Tell us a little bit about him. He was a music teacher.

Ah, yes. He a, he went to the First World War, when he came back, he settled in Chicago. And he worked for the telephone company there as a cabinet maker. And then he taught music on the side. And he used to have different orchestras and bands, not jazz bands, concert bands, that

he took charge of. And our house was always a -- in Blue Island -- was always a scene of rehearsals for the local kids that went to the high school. And Baco would tutor them and teach 'em. And he taught me how to play the euphonium and any of the instruments like the trumpet, the French horn and the bass, anything that had three valves I would play. He taught me all that including piano. My aunt, who was German, taught me piano. And , once I had drums, I had drum lessons from my uncle too.
So he was an all around musician, then.
Yes he was, absolutely.
Oh, did a, did the euphonium that you learned on, was that one of the single bell models or was that one of the double bell models?
Yea, well a baritone is the one that doesn't have a bell on the side, but the euphonium, I think, is the one that's that has a bell on the side. Now I was using, I was using the euphonium.
What about the valve trombone, did you learn that at the time?
No, I, I didn't, I didn't play any trombone until I went out west.
Oh, I see that, the trombone came much later then.
Yes, much later.

I see. Did -- does the name Walter Dyett, Captain Walter Dyett ring a bell? It was -- do you thing that your uncle might have known him? He was a music teacher in Chicago, and he taught at the Du Sable High School for many, many years. From a -- this may have been a little after the, the time that you were studying with your uncle, but he studied and taught there from about the '20s into the 1950s.
What did he play?
I believe he played all the instruments, because so many musicians out of Chicago, older and younger musicians, have mentioned his name.
Well, I heard my uncle mention somebody by the name of Dyack.
Dyach . . .
I think he's a Ukaranian.(sic)
Oh, a Ukraniam musician. No, this was a black musician.
Oh, oh,oh,oh. Well then it's not the same party. No I don't; I can't recall.
I see. Ok, so how did things go in Chicago? I mean, you went to school there and in the Chicago area, and you
studied there. Did you like it? Did it take some getting used to?

Yes, at first it was nice to a, to be away. It's always nice for a change, but, after awhile, you get a, get used to different little odds and ends that happens to you. And like , like you're always one of, when you're in school you're always the last to be selected on a, on a, a team or anything like that. And I, I, I went through our -- in Chicago I began to realize the prejudices that people have against one another. And I became aware of it, and I didn't, I didn't try to, try to be any different from what I was. My Indianness never left me, but I have fought through difference where it may have hurt somebody else, but it never hurt me at all because I always have the attitude that I'm just good as you. You know, that's the only way you can get around in this world. Or you think you're better than me; I, I think I'm just as good as you.
. . . just as good as you.

You know, that's, that's the way I am. I mean all through my life, like I'll be blowin' my horn, and I - here's some guy blowin'; he's probably out blowing me. And , and I psych myself; I say to myself I'm just as good as him. Although, he may be out blowing me. No. And then the - when I'm out blowin' somebody else, I always praise them because it's an accepted thing that in order to get along in this
world you have to praise the other guy whether he's better than you or he's not as well, as, as a good player as you are. You praise them too.

That's being fair and open and not creating jealousies and that sort of thing, which prevails so much in, in life. You, your uncle's training, getting back to him, it was a very rigorous schedule and training and so forth. Did he have you doing any particular exercises in learning music that you - that are outstanding?
Yes, he gave me all kind of exercises in , in trumpet playing...because that was his main instrument. Every morning, before breakfast, we had to play the long tones, and . . .
Before breakkfast!

Before breakfast, we used to play long tones. He'd be off to work, and I'd be off to school. That's how I, I learned. And then, my aunt would set me on the piano: set next, she sat next to me, and I'd be looking out, out the, out the window, and the kids would be play- ing baseball; I want to get out there, and my mind is ten miles away. And a, in fact, in fact my goodness, in fact where - when my aunt would know that I wasn't paying attention, she would kind of slap me, behind me, behind the ear. She practically drove music into me
too. And I got a lot of respect for my aunt Mary because she taught me as much piano as she could, and then I had to go to get another teacher.
I see. After school did you, after classes were over at school, did you play in a school orchestra, or did you come home and practice more?

Well, I did play in the - while I was in the grade school in Blue Island, I played the high school concert band. And one time there was an abundance of trumpet players, and I had been playing trumpet the year before. So, the band leader, band master would come and ask me, he said, 'Russell, there's so many trumpet players, would like to play something else?' I said, 'Sure.' So I played the bass; then I played the euphonium, and I never learned trombone at all. I didn't care for trombone because my time was taken up with those instruments with the three valves.
I see.
That's how it . . .
Ok. How about; well, let's see. You left your uncle's house when you were a teenager. What a -- and then you went into Chicago proper. What were some of the circumstances?
Yes. When I was beginning to realize that I was

somewhat out of place in Blue Island, I began to thing of home. I was homesick. And I did not leave home because because of so much pre judice as to I was beginning to be aware that I need to be at home in Arizona, you know. That's where I belong. I wanted to go back home. And our different uncles and aunts had problems at home with my aunt and uncle and my brother, so I said well I'd just better cut out. So, I left home. My school was out in the summer of 1930. Yes. I . . .
Yes.
Well, this is when you went back to - you were going to go back to Arizona or when you left your uncle's?
I did go back to Arizona that -- during that summer. No. I, I think it was '29. I'm not too sure is it rather. But a, I left home . . .
This was before you heard Louis Armstrong.
Oh yes.
Yea.
I didn't know who Louis Armstrong was. And a, I'm gettin' to that. When I left Blue Island, I went to Chicago and just roamed the streets trying to find myself

and how to get back to Arizona. And at that time I was in the Hundred Twenty-Fourth Field Artillery Band, the National Guard across from White Sox Park on Wentworth Avenue. And a, when I roamed the streets of Chicago, I didn't have any job or any money, and I was begging food and trying to survive, and I was sleeping in a burned-out coffin factory. And I would go to sleep in a coffin with excelsor that is in there and cover myself for warmth.
And you were almost playing like a Count Dracula during that time. How the . . .

I'm telling you; it was rough. And when you mean rough, it means rough. It -- I always figure, figure that my ..... someday my ship will come in. And I'm beginning to, at that time beginning to see the dawn comin' up by listening in front of the Sunset Cafe and hearing this trumpet blowing through the walls. It looks like the wall's gonna crumble. And I wasn't the only one in front of the Sunset. There was other people that came back -- they didn't have the money to go in -- just listening, just, just listen and see who was blowin'. About the second or a third night I was there, I finally got nerve enough to ask one of the listeners outside in the sidewalk. I said, 'Who was that blowing?' And a -- 'Oh you don't know? There, I'll show you.' He took me over in front of the place, and I saw the picture, and under the picture with the horn, the trumpet, under there was the

name, Louis Armstrong. Mind you, this wasn't really, this was way before he was called Sachmo, but as we know him now, he's Sachmo. But at that time, I heard, when I heard Louis, that was the most beautiful he, he -- I, I was more determined to be a jazz musician. I think I and, and many, many musicians have used Lou Armstrong as our base -- our, their main reason to be in jazz because of the way that -- oh, here I come with the projection again -- the way he was projected by singing, by his improvisations and by the rhythms. That's personality. There, there isn't anything out of, out of the ordinary to -- that, that, that won't describe Armstrong. He, he's a prince. He's, he's one of the greatest. I mean . . .
SIDE "B"
Ok. So, you were around fourteen or fifteen or sixteen at this time. You were -- of course we . . .
No, no. When I was seventeen, Louis was twenty-nine.
He was born in 1900 on the fourth of July.
Yes, and I was born in 1912.
On August the thirteenth.
Yes, right. And so at twenty-nine -- in 1929 I
was seventeen, and, I may be wrong cause I'm just, I'm goin' by hear-say, Louis must have been twenty-nine in twenty-nine, of course, because a . . .
Yea.

Anyway, through my a, I mean, my experience was in Chicago. I have many memories of the good days and the bad days, the rough days. I once, on the south side on State Street, saw an ad for railroad people to work on the railroad in Indiana, Michigan, everywhere and all the states in the midwest, and I went over there to apply for a job. And the -- so, to make a long story short, they send me to the west side of Chicago, and I was stamping on the railroad. And I'm not used to hard work like that. So, after I worked about maybe four hours, a man came to me and said to me, he said, 'How old are you?' I said I was 27, you know, like a big man, you know.
Uh-huh.

So he said, 'I don't think you're used to hard work because a -- I think you'd better go and go get your time.' That's how I lost that job after working for, for four hours. They knew that I was, I was, I was not twenty-seven. I was only seventeen at the time and I have done anything -- didn't do any work. So, back to the south-side Chicago, and I walked the streets of Chicago. And one time, one time I ran into
some woman by the name of Gypsy. Well, Gypsy was in the, oh, the world's oldest profession.
Uh-huh.

And he thought I -- she thought I was in for a good time. So, she took me upstairs to her appartment, and, so, I opened my heart to her. I said, "I'm sorry, but I have no money. I have no job. If you could let me sleep here, I can, I can clean the house for you or wash windows or wash dishes or wash everything. I want earn my keep." And I guess she put me under her wing, you know, big hearted. Those type of ladies are very good hearted. So, she said, "I'm gonna ask my husband. Let's go back downstairs." And so, we went out there, and here is her husband in a carriage with a baby. And so, they talked it over for a while and then says, "All right, let him go up and scrub, scrub the floors, regular, and let's see how he makes out." So, I existed in that manner for just about a week or two weeks, but a, it shows the times that I have had. And I, I once, I once was arrested for a just investigation, and I got, I got throwed in with the worst characters of the city on the South side, there. And I was let go the next morning, just investigating. And then, I would walk to, to the loop with Chicago, and I see the, the different theaters, the famous bands as come through. Jean Goldkette, Wayne King, Ted Lewis and many, many famous big names. Coon-Sanders was right

there at the Black Hawk, and I used to hear them over the radio, and I was exposed to that. And one time I walked all the way from the Loop to Lincoln Park on west side of Chicago, and I heard a band, a famous band called the Rhythm Kings. And, I'm pretty sure at that time and to this day, there must have been some famous musicians in there, to this day that -- but I didn't know them then. And a . . .
Was it the New Orleans Rhythm Kings . . .
I wonder which one, which one that were Chicago Rhythm Kings were.
Or there were Chicago Rhythm Kings.

Yea, I think that's, that was, that was them. And, between that and then -- I would still go back to Blue Island to visit my brother, and we talked about the old days in, in a -- on the reservation. How our, our language began. We can't remember our language because we didn't have no occassion to talk anymore Pima. And I told him that I could sing our chants like Old Skomuck during when we were, we were kids on the reservation.

I see. That was quite a traumatic time for you then, dealing with the fact that you wern't remembering the language because you weren't using it, and also traveling around Chicago and seeing some of the names of the musicians and
the famous band leaders on the marquees. You never got a chance to hear them, I guess, at that time.

No, no I didn't because, as I said, I, I go back, I went back to the re -- not the reser -- to Blue Island to, to visit my, my brother, and that one time my uncle ran into me, and he said to me it was gettin' on to school time in September. So he asked me what I wanted to go to school, or you want to go home. So I said I want to go home. So my uncle said, "All right, I'll buy you a ticket." And his advice to me was "go back to school when you get home." So that's how I came back to Arizona. And talk about trauma! At that time when I got into Arizona, I was let out at Tucson. My mother had remarried, and I want to -- when we had a meal at the table, I asked, I asked the name of the salt in Pima -- the name of this in Pima, the name of this in Pima. And, talk about trauma, I just broke down and said I'm sorry I can't remember my language, you know. And they begin to know that -- realize that I been through a trauma about living the two types of lives like in Chicago and back to Arizona with the Indians. And, at that time, I used to go to the stores in Tucson and listen to records in the music stores. And I used to hear Guy Lombardo and Meyer Davis and quite a number of famous bands through records, and I always imitated them. Once again, imitation. That was the -- that's why, to this day, I, I, I don't copy anybody, but I try to use my own, my own way of

playing, performing. And those years in Tucson was very instructive. I'm gettin' back to where I came from. I find myself temporarily where I came from, and in that way, I begin to be a little more aware of who I was, and my Indian-ness has never left me although I was away from the Indians in Chicago and I had forgotten my language.
You went to Tucson High School there, and how was it as far as your playing music? You started playing the trombone at that time?

Yes. I tell ya how I got to the trombone. I, I went to the band master in Tucson High School, and they were all filled up, every instrument, and I couldn't, I couldn't join the concert band. So they said, "However, we have an opening for a trombonist if you play trombone, we have a opening for a -- in the orchestra." So I said, I said, "Well, I know, I know how to play trombone ,but I got a good back-ground. I don't think it'll take long for me to play trombone." And incidentally, there was another Pima Indian in the Tuscon High School Orchestra, and a very distant relative. The name is Walker. And, well I, I got a -- my brother bought me a $12 trombone. And I'll never forget that. I started with the trombone in the high school orchestra, although I didn't know a thing about it, but I could play the other instruments, and all I had to do was learn the positions and get my embouchure for the trombone. That was my first introduction to the trombone. I have never left it until now.

What kinds of music -- you were able to a, get into the concert band that they had, or was it a marching band that they had? What kinds of musical aggregations a, did they have that you performed in actually, once you started getting the trombone down?

Well, I didn't, perform any, any -- I wasn't good enough. I was good enough to be in the orchestra in the high school, but I didn't get to playing jazz until I -- that year, 1930. it was the year 1930 when my step-father died, and I said I might as well go to the Indian school. And that'd be one, one mouth less to feed because I always did eat, you know. I didn't . . . Anyway, I applied to Sherman Institute at Riverside, California, and they accepted me. Phoenix was full. I couldn't get to Phoenix, so this time I went to Sherman Institute at Riverside. And that's where I started the jazz trombone. And I would play jazz in my dormitory, and all the kids would be listening there. Then they're egging me on, 'Play more; play more.'

Who were, at the time -- Louis certainly inspired you musically, but were there any trombonists that you were aware of, through recordings or what have you, that you liked, and that also inspired you?
I'm sorry to say I didn't have any, any -- I didn't follow anybody because I was too busy going to school. But I, learned there how to play jazz.
You know, ever since then -- I think it was the memories of, of that -- I . . .
Chicago?

Yes, memories of Chicago and Louis Armstrong that kept me in jazz. And I . . . begin my own improvisations, and I, I would -- whenever in the trombone, I begin to think of jazz a little -- more in a directly, so to speak, I, I, I wanted, wanted to be a jazz musician in the worst way possible, even then when I was goin' to school. And when I went to school there, there used to be some Mexican bands around Chino, California and Corona, California. And they would come and pick me up to play at the dances. And in that way, I used to make my little bread, my money outside of school. And I was pretty well known as the jazz coming up, up and coming jazz man of the year.

"The jazz trombonist" of Riverside, California. So, you really began to attract some attention there then. That's remarkable.
